findings.title: Unrelated and unexplained change of cleanup ticker interval from 10 to 1 minute
findings.body: The periodic ticker that drives srv.clean() (which runs all cleanup jobs: temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) was changed from `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)`. This is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (splitting annotation cleanup queries to avoid MySQL deadlocks) and is not mentioned anywhere in the PR description. Running every cleanup job 10x more frequently increases database load across every cleanup job, not just annotations, and could even make the targeted deadlock problem worse by increasing contention frequency. This looks like a leftover debugging change that should be reverted or, if intentional, needs to be called out and justified in the PR description.

findings.title: Misuse of Error log level for routine, successful batch cleanup logging
findings.body: In CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags, every batch iteration logs via r.log.Error (e.g. lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) even when there is no error (err is nil and is logged as a field). This mislabels routine, expected operational information as an error, which will pollute error-level logs/alerting dashboards that filter or page on Error severity, and may trigger false alerts in production for normal cleanup activity. These should be logged at Debug or Info level, consistent with how the rest of the cleanup service (cleanup.go) logs routine completion at Debug level.

findings.title: Inefficient O(n^2) string building for SQLite large-batch delete
findings.body: In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a batch size exceeding the parameter limit, the code builds the IN-clause value list by repeatedly calling fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop over all ids. Each call reallocates and copies the growing `values` string, making this O(n^2) in the number of ids. With batch sizes in the tens of thousands (the added test uses 32767), this can be noticeably slow and allocate excessive memory compared to using a strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt into a byte slice (as is already done elsewhere in this same file, e.g. in getAccessControlFilter).
